description: Count the contour lines across an elevation range with the Contour Line Count Calculator — relief divided by interval, index lines included. Free.

quick_answer: The Contour Line Count Calculator estimates how many contour intervals fit inside an elevation range: relief divided by the contour interval. Enter the lowest and highest elevations and the map's interval and read the line count — the quick way to judge a topo map's density before you open it.

Students grasp intervals when the count is arithmetic: range first, interval second, divide. The calculator makes the lesson self-checking.
USGS 7.5-minute quads use intervals from 5 to 100 ft depending on terrain; the same ground at two intervals gives two very different line counts — and reading experiences.

Relief 3,900 ft (a valley floor at 1,100 ft, a summit at 5,000 ft) at a 30 ft interval: 3,900 ÷ 30 = 130 intervals. One hundred and thirty lines between bottom and top — expect a steep, tightly banded sheet.
A European 1:25,000 sheet with 1,200 m of relief and a 20 m interval: 60 intervals. Same arithmetic, rounder numbers — intervals are chosen per terrain, not per country.

popular_table.title: Common contour intervals (USGS practice)
popular_table.intro: Intervals are picked so a quad stays readable — flat land gets fine slices, mountains get coarse ones.
popular_table.note: Every fifth line is an index contour (heavier, labelled with its elevation) — the count here includes them; they are lines too, just louder ones.

faq: What if the range does not divide evenly?

The remainder means the topmost interval is partial — a summit area inside the last band rather than a line at the very top. Lines drawn equal floor(relief ÷ interval) full crossings plus the boundary lines the map actually prints, which is why the count is stated as intervals.
Yes — closed contours with tick marks (hachures) count the same way; a crater or sink adds its rings to the total exactly like a hill.
What interval do USGS quads use most?
20 ft and 40 ft are the workhorses for 7.5-minute quads in the lower 48; flat coastal sheets drop to 5 or 10 ft so the land gets any lines at all.
Can I count lines a route crosses instead?
That is this same arithmetic aimed at a path: high minus low along the route, divided by the interval — a lower bound on climbing, since routes dip as well as rise.
Why do some maps use supplementary contours?
In very flat terrain, half-interval dashed lines are added so subtle relief (a levee, a drumlin) does not vanish between full intervals. They are extra information, not part of the standard count.
Intervals of 10 or 20 m are standard on European 1:25,000 series; the division is identical — only the unit changes.
Does a bigger count mean harder hiking?
Not by itself: line count is total relief, while difficulty lives in spacing — lines packed tight mean steep ground. Count tells you how much up exists; spacing tells you how it is arranged.
